description: I’m Asif, a robotics and autonomy software engineer (MES, Lamar University) focused on path planning and ROS2. We’re building an interactive Mars map with terrain-aware route planning for the Martian Map challenge. Goal: a polished, working demo. All skill levels welcome. Looking for: web/3D developers, data visualization, geospatial data, design/video, and a space science or writing person. Message me on the team page before Nov 14.
summary:
A map, and a terrain-aware route planner for the rover and the Martian. Martian Autonomy is a survival guide for the first crew on Mars. It places two habitats on checked ground: an ice colony at AP-1 in Arcadia-Amazonis, where ice lies less than 1 m deep, and a sun colony beside InSight in Elysium Planitia. From them it plans roads to all 17 landing sites and planned sites. Every road is routed on NASA MOLA 463 m terrain with steep ground blocked, and checked for loose dust with TES thermal inertia. Around each habitat, suited Marswalk zones show how far a crew member can walk and still get back, measured on HiRISE and CTX terrain.

The result is a sol-by-sol plan: Habitat 1 drives 18,499 km in 289 sols, Habitat 2 18,772 km in 282 sols, with robots pre-placing 46 supply depots. Both fit the calm half of the Mars year. The web map layers roads, stops, dust, slopes, climate, radiation and a live mission panel over real CTX and HiRISE images. It shows that open NASA data can already plan surface operations at planet scale, and where the real limits are: cruise radiation and robot speed.
details:
What it does: Martian Autonomy is a survival guide in map form for the first crew on Mars. Two crew land and live at two habitats in two missions. Every Mars landing site (Mars 3 to Zhurong) and every planned site (Rosalind Franklin, Tianwen-3 zones, the SpaceX/AP ice sites) belongs to its nearest habitat, and each region is explored by road from its habitat. The map answers four questions: where do they live, where can they drive and walk, how long does it take, and what can go wrong on the way?

How it works:

1. Habitats on checked ground. Habitat 1 (ice colony) sits at AP-1, 39.81N 202.08E, a published near-surface ice site (Luzzi et al. 2025). Habitat 2 (sun colony) sits 1.2 km from InSight. Pads and habitat spots were picked on CTX (22 m) and HiRISE (1 m) terrain models: pad slope 15 degrees or less, habitat 1-2 km from the pad.

2. Marswalks. Around each habitat and at Gale, suited-walking zones show the ground reachable on foot within 1, 2 and 4.5 hours with a safe walk back, using a suited walking model (0.61 m/s on the flat, 24.2 degree hard limit). AP-1 has 49 km2 within 2 hours and 98% pad-quality ground.

3. Roads on real terrain. Pass 1 routes every leg with A* on MOLA global terrain at 5.2 km cells, blocking large crater rims. Pass 2 re-routes each leg on the full 463 m MOLA terrain in a 40 km strip either side, with ground over 12 degrees blocked and loose dust costing double time. Travel time follows slope (12 km/h on the flat, slower uphill and across slopes).

4. Visit order. Habitat 2 drives the shortest closed loop (exact Held-Karp search). Habitat 1 follows a set route that drops an empty 6,258 km plains crossing and drives the Opportunity branch out and back.

5. Soft ground. TES thermal inertia is sampled every 2 km on every road: 3,390 of 41,523 km (8%) is loose dust. A scenario halves speed on dust: Habitat 1 307 sols, Habitat 2 296 sols.

6. Sol-by-sol plan. 8 driving hours per sol, a rest sol after 6 driving sols, 5 research sols per site, a camp every night, and a supply depot every 800 km placed by robots before the crew arrives.

7. Mission context. Season (start at the northern spring equinox, finish before the dust season), radiation dose from Curiosity's RAD detector, measured weather from InSight and Viking 2, a launch-window calendar, and a 30-sol short-stay option.

Results: Habitat 1 (ice colony): 9 sites, 18,499 km, 289 sols, 196 camps, 23 depots, steepest road cell 11.9 degrees, about 190 mSv on the route. Habitat 2 (sun colony): 7 sites plus InSight, 18,772 km, 282 sols, 205 camps, 23 depots, steepest road cell 12.0 degrees, about 185 mSv. A 4,252 km link road joins the habitats. Both routes fit the 372-sol calm half of the Mars year and a 500-sol stay.

What we found: the roads are not the hard part. The flight is: a 180-day cruise each way (about 662 mSv) already exceeds NASA's 600 mSv career limit. Robots are the second limit: to pre-place depots in time, a robot must average about 16 km per sol, about 39 times Perseverance's best single sol.

Benefits and impact: a mission planner, student or member of the public can follow each crew sol by sol, see every road over real orbital images, and check every number against its source. It shows that open NASA data is already enough to plan surface logistics at planet scale, and shows where it is not.

User experience: a full-screen map with two coloured routes, numbered stops and a play button. While it plays, a live mission panel shows each crew's activity, leg, distance, next stop, sites visited, position and radiation. Zooming in swaps the relief map for CTX photos and sharp HiRISE close-ups at 24 sites. Switches cover the 30-sol stay, the dust scenario, the dust map and the slope maps. On a phone the panel becomes a bottom sheet.

Tools: Python (NumPy, SciPy sparse-graph Dijkstra, GDAL, Pillow), Leaflet web map, Playwright for testing at laptop and phone sizes, GitHub Pages hosting. Processing ran on a Lenovo Legion desktop. Code and full write-up: https://github.com/Asif-Ucchwas/martian_autonomy

Limits we state openly: craters under about 1.5 km and boulders need HiRISE checks on final approaches. Each road ends 0.3-3 km from its site; that last stretch is drawn dashed and is not slope-checked. Rover speed on dust is assumed. The mission calendar is a scenario, not a NASA schedule. Depot mass and robot power are not modelled.

Use of AI: built with AI assistance (Claude, Anthropic) for code, research summaries and text, as stated in the README and in every script header. All map imagery is NASA/USGS data; no AI-generated images and no NASA branding are used.
